source.title: When Safety Speaks a Language: A Mechanistic Analysis of Safety-Language Identity Entanglement in LLMs

record.tranche_reason: The study measures similarity among safety and language-identity features across languages within individual models. It does not test convergence between models’ representations of the same inputs, or convergence with model scale, seeds, modalities, or performance.
record.gate_note: The reported feature-similarity results below are adjacent to the claim but concern safety-feature sharing across languages within a model, not the convergence behavior named by the claim versions. The authors also discuss prior work on cross-lingual safety transfer; results cited from that work are not included.
record.test_reason: The study compares SAE safety features against language-identity features, and across languages, inside each of three models. It never compares representations of the same inputs between models, seeds or modalities, and it has no scale or capability axis. The only cross-model link is an assumption: Gemma base-model SAEs are applied to Gemma-2-9B-IT, citing Kissane et al. and Gemma Scope. Nothing here tests that transfer, so no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that safety–language entanglement is architecture-dependent: high in late layers for Llama and Qwen, largely disentangled in Gemma. Cross-lingual safety-feature sharing peaks in middle layers, decoupled from where safety signals peak, and English is the most isolated language. Decoder-cosine entanglement predicts the language-identity and fluency costs of SAE safety interventions. Using features orthogonal to language preserves the output language but gives weaker safety gains.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses SAE feature overlap and decoder cosine to analyze safety-language relationships; it does not apply the original representation-convergence method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported feature relationships can look different under Jaccard overlap and decoder cosine similarity.

fits_no_version.finding: Within each model, safety-feature sharing across languages and safety–language entanglement vary by architecture and layer. ID-level overlap (Jaccard) and decoder-direction similarity diverge: for example, Qwen HI harm has Jaccard 0.090 but decoder cosine 0.570.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-lingual safety-feature sharing within instruction-tuned LLMs depends on architecture, layer and similarity metric.

record.problems: The study covers three model families and eight languages, uses top-k (k=5) MI-selected features, and notes that its results may not generalize to other model sizes or alignment procedures. Its intervention experiments target top-5 features at a single layer per experiment. These limitations concern the study’s safety-language analysis; it does not directly test the catalog claim.
record.rows_left_out: Other per-language and language-pair measurements in Appendix D and Appendix E are not listed because they concern safety-feature sharing across languages within a model, not any claim version’s target behavior.

untested.parts: All: no cross-model alignment and no scale or capability axis.
All: no vision models and no paired image-caption data.
All: no models of the same architecture trained from different seeds.
All: no mapping or stitching between models. Base-to-IT SAE transfer for Gemma is assumed from prior work, not tested.
All: features are not matched across models; the cross-model comparisons cover only peak-layer patterns.
All: the Jaccard vs decoder-cosine divergence concerns within-model feature sets, not between-model convergence.
All: no measure of between-model alignment.

record.verdict_notes: Relation is set to 'assumes' only because the Gemma analysis relies on base-model SAEs transferring to the instruction-tuned model, a related cross-model representation-similarity result cited from prior work. That result is about fine-tuned variants of one model, not independently trained models, and is not tested here. The paper does not cite either original source. Every row correctly has versions ['none'].

versions.untested_parts: Model scale, capability, and alignment between independently trained models.
Vision-language alignment on paired images and captions as model performance changes.
Representational convergence across random initializations of the same architecture.
Mapping or stitching representations between models, including relative representations or unpaired mappings.
Recurrence of interpretable features or circuits across different models.
Metric and input dependence of convergence between models on the same data; the study compares metrics for safety-feature relationships across languages instead.
Whether convergence between models is incomplete or explained by shared training data or objectives.
